anglo-american-axis: Citibank's 42.8 per cent of the New York Fed's stock is a holding in the institution that lends to Citibank and inspects it, and an arrangement like that settles decisions among people who already depend on each other. In 1925 that came down to two men: Strong and Norman wanted sterling back on gold, and the $200 million gold credit and Morgan's $100 million for the British government followed, with no voter in either country asked. The money committed in a credit like that belongs to the public standing behind each central bank. Central banks lending each other reserves is ordinary business, the shareholdings are on the public record, and the Fed and the Bank of England have kept a published standing swap line since 31 October 2013. What the ownership and the shared London partnerships change is who is in the room when a decision is taken.
central-bankers-clubs: The rules deciding how much of a bank's own money must stand behind its loans are drafted inside an institution that cannot be sued in Swiss courts, cannot have its archives read, and is checked by a private firm rather than a national audit office, so no outside court or auditor can ask to see the working. When a capital rule turns out to be too thin, the bank that fails is rescued at home and the loss lands on its depositors and the national budget, not on the committee that set the number. Immunities of this kind go to other international bodies as well, so that a host country cannot lean on an institution holding other countries' reserves, and the Basel standards themselves are published. The Group of Thirty seats serving central bankers beside private bankers from the firms their rules apply to.
cfa-franc-zone: Unlimited convertibility at a fixed rate means importers and savers in the zone avoid the currency swings neighbouring countries live with, and it means the rate is not theirs to set. On 12 January 1994 France devalued the CFA franc by 50 per cent, and anyone holding the currency that morning found it bought half as much from abroad as the day before. The reserves work the same way: they sit in an account at the French Treasury, and the return on them is set by the institution holding them, about 40 million euros a year to the BCEAO in 2018-2019. The guarantee is not free for France, which has to supply euros whenever the zone needs them, and that obligation is the stated reason for the deposits. Since the 2019 agreement France has left the West African boards while still guaranteeing the currency.
banknote-printer-bribery: A note-printing contract is worth years of fees and is settled by a handful of officials rather than in public, so a payment to one of them can decide it. The OeBS managers padded the contracts by 20 per cent for Azerbaijan and 14 per cent for Syria and routed the extra back to the people who chose them, and that padding came out of the buying central bank's own funds, which is public money. The public in Azerbaijan, Syria, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal learned of it from Austrian and Australian courtrooms rather than from their own institutions. Very few firms can print notes that are hard to forge, and a central bank owning its printer is one way a country keeps currency production at home. The De La Rue investigation over South Sudan was closed without charges.
finance-revolving-door: A supervisor judging whether a bank is sound, or whether to prop up a market, is judging firms where former colleagues work and where the next job may be: Robert Kaplan went from Goldman Sachs partner to running the Dallas Fed and back to Goldman as vice chairman in 2024. Nobody has to be bribed for that to matter. If the judgement is soft, the bill goes to depositors, to borrowers paying higher rates afterwards and to taxpayers funding a rescue. It is not one firm either, with entries to the Fed from Carlyle, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup and exits to BlackRock, PIMCO, Citadel, UBS, Commerzbank and Brookfield. The number of people who have worked in the markets a central bank operates in is small, which is the reason usually given for hiring them, and every appointment listed above was made in public.
weaponized-reserves: Reserves held as entries at the New York Fed, the Bank of England or Euroclear can be switched off by the host government with an administrative decision and no court: about $9.5 billion of Afghanistan's central bank in 2021, and 31 tonnes of Venezuelan gold withheld in London since 2019. What is frozen is the money behind the currency and the banking system, so the people who feel it are the ones holding that currency and queuing at those banks, rather than the officials a measure is aimed at. Reserves sit in those three places because that is where markets are deep enough to sell into and custodians do not fail, and the freezes are imposed through published law, generally after an invasion or over a disputed government. The EU has kept the right to use Russia's immobilised assets to repay a 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine.
swap-line-blocs: A central bank with no swap line has to find dollars by selling reserves or letting its currency fall, which raises the price of imported fuel, food and medicine for everyone in the country and the repayment cost for every household and business holding a dollar loan. That was the position of Russia, Turkey, India, Chile, Hungary and Iceland in 2007-2008, while 14 other central banks drew on Fed lines peaking at $583 billion. Since 31 October 2013 five central banks have had permanent lines, so for them the question is settled in advance; for everyone else it is decided when the crisis arrives. The lines exist because a dollar shortage abroad reaches US banks within days, the loans are repaid with interest, and the amounts are published. The People's Bank of China's 32 yuan lines give countries off the Fed's list somewhere else to ask.
gulf-dollar-pegs: Holding a fixed rate to the dollar means keeping the local interest rate close to the Fed's, so households and firms in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar borrow on terms set in Washington for American conditions. The 1974 Jeddah arrangement ran the other way: Saudi Arabia bought US Treasuries through 'add-ons' outside the public auctions, and the size stayed secret for 41 years, so American voters could not see how much of their government's debt one foreign government held and Saudi citizens could not see where that much of the oil income had gone. The figure, about $117 billion, came out in 2016. A country that sells its main export for dollars has a plain reason to price its currency in dollars, since it keeps export earnings and domestic prices in step, and Kuwait's switch to a basket in May 2007 shows the arrangement can be undone.
independence-law-wave: A law of this kind stops a government ordering the central bank to print money for its deficit or cut rates before an election, and it also means that when the bank raises rates, the higher mortgage payments and the lost jobs fall on people with no one to vote out over it. Governments with direct access to the printing press have paid their bills by issuing money, and the price of that is inflation, which takes its cut from wages and savings; that is the reason given for the laws. Many of them were not local decisions, since the reforms follow IMF loan programmes and EU treaty articles 130-131 require independence before a country can join the euro. So the law often arrives as a condition of a loan or of membership rather than as something an electorate chose.
banking-crisis-waves: A systemic rescue moves the losses of a failing bank off the people who owned it and lent to it and onto the state, which lets a bank lend on terms it would not risk carrying alone. The bills reach 55.1 per cent of a year's national output in Argentina in 1980 and 37.6 per cent in Iceland and Ireland in 2008, and sums that size come out of taxes, out of borrowing serviced for years, and out of spending that then does not happen on anything else. The short-run alternative is worse, because if the payments system stops then wages are not paid and firms cannot settle their accounts. That is why treasuries and central banks keep doing it, and why a bank large enough to take the system with it can plan on being rescued.
governor-removal-wave: A governor who can be replaced at will sets interest rates knowing it, which gives a leader who wants cheaper borrowing a way to get it without changing any law. Turkiye's four replacements by decree between July 2019 and June 2023 followed disputes over rates. When the rate is set to fit a government's calendar, the effect reaches people through the currency and the price of imported goods, and savings held in that currency are worth whatever the policy leaves them worth. Not every removal is improper: terms end, governors are dismissed for failures of their own, and an unelected official overriding an elected government is itself a problem, which is the argument made each time. The Lisa Cook case went to the Supreme Court, which in June 2026 let her stay on the board, so that one was decided in court rather than by decree.
lebanon-financial-engineering: Paying commercial banks high returns to bring dollars in and park them at the central bank keeps dollars arriving, which lets a country hold its exchange rate and keep paying out on deposits after the money to do both has gone. The foreign-currency position moved from a $7.2 billion surplus to a $50.7 billion deficit in five years with no loss shown on the balance sheet. Bank Audi and Blom Bank took the largest share of the returns and $111 million left in commissions to recipients the forensic auditors could not name, while depositors learned what the position was when the Alvarez & Marsal audit reported, years after their deposits had been used. Central banks do pay interest to attract foreign currency and defend a rate, and that by itself is standard policy; what the published accounts did not show was the shortfall.
city-of-london-offshore: A company registered in one of these jurisdictions lets money leave a central bank and arrive as property somewhere else with no name attached at either end, which is what Forry Associates did with about $330 million from Banque du Liban between 2002 and 2015. The cost falls on the country the money came from, where it shows up as reserves that are not there and an investigator who cannot establish who owns the company that received them. The territories hosting such companies are not part of the UK, though London handles their defence and foreign relations, and the UK with ten of them accounts for 9.26 per cent of the world's financial secrecy. None of the structure is illegal, and it began as banking business rather than concealment: after the 1957 exchange controls stopped London banks lending sterling to non-residents they lent dollars instead.
big-four-auditors: An audit is the check that tells the public whether a central bank's own accounts are honest, and most central banks buy it from a firm. When that firm also earns fees from the banks the central bank is supposed to police, the same partners depend on both sides of the relationship staying comfortable. Lebanon shows the cost: the 2018 accounts carrying a $6.82 billion asset that did not exist were signed by EY and Deloitte, qualified, and published anyway. The four firms are the ones with the staff and reach to audit an institution of that size, which is why central banks and commercial banks alike keep hiring them. Where a state audit office does the work instead, there is no fee relationship, and the audit sits inside the government being reported on.
supervisory-capture: A supervisor that is slow or deferential costs the public money later, when a bank that should have been stopped has to be rescued. The inquiries above were all written after the collapse they describe, which is the usual order: the deference is visible in documents at the time and acted on afterwards. Two things make it easier to see early. One is whether the supervisor publishes what it found and when, including reviews of its own conduct. The other is what happens to people who say a bank is in trouble before the supervisor does - short sellers, journalists, staff inside the bank. A supervisor investigating those people instead of the bank is a fact that can be checked at the time, not years later.
asset-purchase-programmes: Creating money and buying assets with it is not a transfer to the public; it is a purchase from whoever owns the assets, at a price the buying raises. Three questions decide who gains. Who executes the purchases, and do they sell what is being bought. Whose securities are eligible, which in practice means large firms that issue bonds rather than small firms that borrow from banks. And what the central bank pays on the money it created, because that payment goes to the commercial banks holding the reserves and, where a treasury has indemnified the scheme, is charged to the public. None of this is hidden: the contracts, the eligible-bond lists and the indemnity are published. It is simply spread across documents that are rarely read together.
cbdc-vendors: A digital currency is a claim on the central bank, but the thing people would actually hold is software, and that software is usually written, hosted and maintained by a private company under contract. Three things follow, and all three are visible in the record rather than hypothetical. The money can stop when the vendor's system fails, as it did in the Eastern Caribbean over an expired certificate. The same handful of firms end up supplying many countries, so a decision taken in one contract is reproduced across others. And what the system can see or restrict is a design choice made inside that contract: whether payments are traceable to a person, and whether money can be limited in what it is spent on or when it expires. Those choices are rarely the part that gets announced.
money-routes: For an ordinary person, the cost usually arrives later and looks unrelated: a failed bank's losses covered by public money, or imports priced at a black market rate. A central bank does not need to hand over cash for insiders to gain. Its choices about whom to inspect, rescue, or sell dollars to carry a money value, and that value attracts people who want it. This is why the rules on who gets those decisions, and who can see them, matter as much as the interest rate. Public records of these decisions make favoritism easier to detect.
pressure-routes: Most of this pressure asks for cheaper money now, some for the bank's reserves to cover state bills, and studies tie it to higher inflation afterward, which reaches anyone paying prices or holding savings. Legal protection does not settle the matter, since banks with strong independence laws still report pressure. Pressure from abroad does not need a vote or a court at all: a country whose earnings or payments pass through another power's system can be warned about losing access. The public can learn of such pressure decades late, as with the Nixon tapes, so a central bank's decisions are hard to judge at the time.
money-meets-pressure: Central bank officials can cost powerful people money, by refusing a loan, closing a bank or holding interest rates up. If an accusation alone can remove them, accusations become a way to control them, and the public loses a supervisor willing to act. If they can stop a case by calling it political, public money can be taken without penalty. EU law tries to allow both: prosecutors may proceed against a governor over private acts, while a governor's removal needs evidence a court can check. For a reader, a charge says little until the outcome, the accuser and the timing are known.
